2027-04-15.title: Thursday of the Third Week of Easter
readings: Look, here is water! What is to prevent me from being baptized?
Let all the earth cry out to God with joy (or: Alleluia)
I am the living bread that came down from heaven
2027-04-15.alt: Easter weekday. The Alleluia sounds again at the Gospel acclamation; the Paschal candle is lit at the liturgy until Pentecost; the Regina Caeli takes the place of the Angelus. All this week the Gospel is the Bread of Life discourse of John 6. Liturgical colour: white.
2027-04-15.verse: I am the living bread that came down from heaven. Whoever eats of this bread will live forever; and the bread that I will give for the life of the world is my flesh.
theo: Philip has just seen a whole city rejoice. Now an angel sends him somewhere very different: “Get up and go toward the south to the road that goes down from Jerusalem to Gaza.” Luke adds: “This is a wilderness road.” God sends the evangelist away from the crowd to one man. On the road is an Ethiopian, a eunuch, a court official of the Candace, the queen of the Ethiopians, in charge of her whole treasury. In the Bible “Ethiopia” means the ancient kingdom of Kush, south of Egypt, in today's Sudan; for the people of Jerusalem it was the edge of the known world. This powerful man has travelled well over a thousand kilometres to worship in Jerusalem, and now, seated in his chariot, he is reading the prophet Isaiah aloud, as people did in the ancient world. The Spirit says: “Go over to this chariot and join it.” Philip runs, hears the words, and asks the simple question that begins so many conversions: “Do you understand what you are reading?” The answer is humble and honest: “How can I, unless someone guides me?” The passage is Isaiah's song of the Servant: “Like a sheep he was led to the slaughter, and like a lamb silent before its shearer.” “About whom, may I ask you, does the prophet say this?” And Philip, “starting with this scripture,” proclaims to him the good news of Jesus. They come to water, and the man cries out: “Look, here is water! What is to prevent me from being baptized?” By the old law a eunuch could not enter the assembly of the Lord (Deuteronomy 23:1), but Isaiah had promised that God would give faithful eunuchs “a name better than sons and daughters” (Isaiah 56:3–5). On a desert road that promise is kept. Philip baptizes him, the Spirit snatches Philip away, and the Ethiopian “went on his way rejoicing.” Ancient tradition, cherished in Ethiopia, honours him as one of the first to carry the Gospel to Africa, and the whole Church sees in this story the pattern of Christian initiation: the Scriptures opened, Christ proclaimed, faith, Baptism, and joy.

In the Gospel Jesus says something that should make us humble: “No one can come to me unless drawn by the Father who sent me.” Faith is never simply our achievement. St Augustine says, in substance, that the Father draws us not by force but by delight, as a branch held out draws a sheep, or as a child is drawn by the sight of what it loves. The Father drew the Ethiopian through his love of the Scriptures; he draws us too, often through someone who sits beside us and explains. Jesus quotes Isaiah: “And they shall all be taught by God.” Then he speaks in the present tense: “whoever believes has eternal life.” Eternal life begins now. And then the discourse turns a corner. “Your ancestors ate the manna in the wilderness, and they died.” “I am the living bread that came down from heaven. Whoever eats of this bread will live forever; and the bread that I will give for the life of the world is my flesh.” The word “flesh” is the same word St John used for the Incarnation: “the Word became flesh” (John 1:14). The bread Jesus will give is not a symbol of his flesh; it is his flesh, given “for the life of the world,” that is, offered on the cross. The Eucharist makes present that one sacrifice of Calvary (Catechism 1366–1367). The Ethiopian was reading of a lamb led to the slaughter; at every Mass we receive that Lamb, the living bread who was slain and lives for ever.
outline: Ask: who sat beside me and helped me understand the faith?
God sends the evangelist to one seeker.
Point 2 · How can I, unless someone guides me?
Baptism, and a promise kept to the excluded.
My flesh for the life of the world.
“Whoever eats of this bread will live forever.”
live: Offer to read the Sunday Gospel this week with a child, a godchild or a new Catholic, and explain it simply.
Pray today for the catechist, parent or priest who first opened the Scriptures to you.
2027-04-15.prayer: Father, you sent Philip down the desert road to one seeking heart, and you draw us to your Son by the delight of your love. Open the Scriptures to us, renew in us the joy of our Baptism, and feed us with the living bread, the flesh of Christ given for the life of the world, who lives and reigns with you for ever and ever. Amen. Alleluia.
altar: The Ethiopian read of the Lamb led to the slaughter. On the altar that same Lamb, risen and living, gives us his flesh for the life of the world. This is not a sign of something absent: it is Christ himself, the living bread from heaven.

quick: An angel sent Philip to a desert road, where an Ethiopian official was reading Isaiah.
Philip explained the passage about the Lamb and proclaimed Jesus; the man was baptized and went on his way rejoicing.
Jesus said: I am the living bread; the bread I will give for the life of the world is my flesh.
2027-04-15.action: Read and explain this Sunday's Gospel to someone younger in the faith.
2027-04-15.question: Do I let someone guide me in understanding Scripture, or do I read alone and give up?

family.explain: A rich man from far away Ethiopia was riding home in his chariot, reading the Bible, but he could not understand it. God sent Philip to run beside the chariot! Philip explained that the Bible was speaking about Jesus. The man believed, and when they saw some water he said: here is water, baptize me! He went home full of joy.
family.intention: We pray for people who want to know God but have no one to explain the faith to them.
family.ask: Ask: “Who taught me about Jesus? Let us thank God for them tonight.”

illus: A software engineer in Kochi, raised a Catholic but long uninterested, picked up his grandmother's Malayalam Bible after her funeral because it was full of her pencil marks. He could not make sense of most of it. One evening he asked the elderly sacristan, who was locking the church, what one underlined verse meant. The sacristan sat down on the steps and talked with him until it was dark. They met every Thursday after that. A year later the young man was reading at the Easter Vigil.

pm.open: Lord Jesus, living bread from heaven, draw us to yourself, open the Scriptures to us, and send us on our way rejoicing. Alleluia. Amen.
share: Do you understand what you are reading? How can I, unless someone guides me? (Acts 8:30–31). Who has been a Philip for me, and for whom can I be one?
Look, here is water! What is to prevent me from being baptized? (Acts 8:36). What do I think keeps people away from Christ, and is it real?
The bread that I will give for the life of the world is my flesh (John 6:51). How do I prepare to receive the living bread?
pm.resp: Let all the earth cry out to God with joy. Alleluia.
interc: For catechists, teachers of Scripture and all who sit beside seekers to explain the faith.
For the Christians of Africa, and for the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church, that we may grow in unity.
For those who feel excluded from the people of God, that they may find a welcome.
For the newly baptized, that they may go on their way rejoicing.
For our group, that our hunger for the living bread may grow.
pm.close: Father, you draw all people to your Son. Make us patient guides and joyful witnesses, and feed us with the bread of eternal life. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.

homily: Dear friends, Philip was busy with a great mission in Samaria, and God sent him to a desert road for one man. The Lord does not only care for crowds. He will send an evangelist across a desert for a single seeking heart.

That man was reading Isaiah and could not understand it. When Philip asked: do you understand what you are reading?, he answered: how can I, unless someone guides me? (Acts 8:31). Many people today are like him: they have a Bible, or a memory of the faith, but no one to sit beside them. You could be that Philip for someone.

Philip started from the passage about the Lamb led to the slaughter and told him about Jesus. Then they came to water, and the man said: look, here is water! What is to prevent me from being baptized? (Acts 8:36). The man the old law had kept outside was welcomed into God's family. He went on his way rejoicing.

In the Gospel Jesus says: I am the living bread that came down from heaven; the bread that I will give for the life of the world is my flesh (John 6:51). The Lamb the Ethiopian read about is the Bread we receive. Let us come to him with faith, and then go out like that man from Africa, on our way rejoicing. Alleluia. Amen.
kids: Children, a man was reading the Bible in his chariot, but he did not understand it. God sent Philip to help him. Philip told him about Jesus, and the man was baptized and was so happy! Whenever you do not understand something about Jesus, ask your parents, your teacher or Father. God loves it when we ask!

intro: Theme: “I am the living bread that came down from heaven.”
A desert road, a seeker who needed a guide, water for Baptism, and the flesh of Christ given for the life of the world.

points.h: How can I, unless someone guides me?
sub: God sends Philip to one man.
Starting from the Scripture, proclaiming Jesus.
q: So they read from the book, from the law of God, with interpretation. They gave the sense, so that the people understood the reading.

So Philip ran up to it and heard him reading the prophet Isaiah. He asked, “Do you understand what you are reading?” He replied, “How can I, unless someone guides me?” And he invited Philip to get in and sit beside him.
points.apply: Choose one person this week with whom you will read and talk over a passage of the Gospel.

sub: The man the law kept outside.
A name better than sons and daughters.
q: Do not let the foreigner joined to the LORD say, “The LORD will surely separate me from his people”; and do not let the eunuch say, “I am just a dry tree.”
As they were going along the road, they came to some water; and the eunuch said, “Look, here is water! What is to prevent me from being baptized?”
points.apply: Ask yourself honestly whom you would rather keep outside the Church, and pray for them by name.

sub: My flesh for the life of the world.
q: He humbled you by letting you hunger, then by feeding you with manna, with which neither you nor your ancestors were acquainted, in order to make you understand that one does not live by bread alone, but by every word that comes from the mouth of the LORD.
I am the living bread that came down from heaven. Whoever eats of this bread will live forever; and the bread that I will give for the life of the world is my flesh.
points.apply: Make a spiritual communion each day this week, especially on days you cannot go to Mass.

concl: God goes out of his way for a single seeker and opens the Scriptures through those who walk beside him.
The Lamb of whom Isaiah spoke is the living bread, his flesh given for the life of the world.
2027-04-15.resolve: Read one Gospel passage this week with someone younger in the faith, and pray for the person who first taught you.
